name: B2B workspace
when: CRMs, admin panels, project and ticket tools, internal back-offices: people who come back every day to work through records.

actors.who: The person who works through records all day: a sales rep, a support agent, a coordinator.
questions: Which single task do they repeat most in a day, and how many times?
How many records do they handle per day, and how many are open at once?
On which device and where do they do it: a desk, a phone between meetings, a site visit?
What words do they use for the records and states, as opposed to the words the database uses?
What do they switch to outside the product to finish a task (phone, email, chat, spreadsheet)?
What makes them lose their place: an interruption, a page reload, a filter that resets?

actors.who: The person who sets the product up for others: permissions, fields, imports, reports.
questions: Which settings do they change after the first week, and how often?
Who do they answer to for what the team sees in reports?
What happens today when a permission or a field is set wrong, and who notices?

screens.name: Sign in
screens.does: Gets into their own workspace and lands where they left off.

screens.name: First run (empty)
screens.does: Understands what goes here and creates or imports the first record.

screens.name: Record list
screens.does: Finds the record they need by searching, filtering or sorting, and opens it.

screens.name: Record detail
screens.does: Reads the record and takes the next action on it without leaving the screen.

screens.name: Create or edit record
screens.does: Enters or corrects the record's data once, with errors caught before they save.

screens.name: Overview dashboard
screens.does: Sees what needs attention today and goes straight to it.

screens.name: Settings
screens.does: Changes how the workspace behaves and sees that the change took effect.

journeys.goal: Get from sign-up to the first useful record
watch: The empty state says what goes here and offers the one action that starts it.
Count the steps from landing to the first saved record; every step must earn its place.
After saving, the new record is visible where the person expects it, without a reload.

journeys.goal: Find one record and take the next action on it
watch: The primary action on the detail screen is reachable without scrolling at a phone viewport.
Every action shows a change within a second; anything longer shows progress.
Going back to the list keeps the search, filter and scroll position.

journeys.goal: See what needs attention today and clear it
watch: Numbers on the overview link to the records behind them.
After acting on a record, the overview reflects the change when the person returns.
Nothing on the overview needs a legend the screen does not show.

journeys.goal: Change one setting and confirm it applied
watch: The setting says what it changes before it is saved.
A destructive or team-wide change names its consequence and can be undone or is confirmed.
The effect is visible on the screen it changes.

research: What is the domain's own vocabulary for records, stages and outcomes, and where is it written down?
Which regulations or audit rules apply to the data (personal data, retention, who may see what)?
Which competing or adjacent tools do these teams already use, and what do people praise or complain about in their reviews?
What volume and speed does the work have: records per day, time allowed per record, peak hours?
What does a mistake cost in this domain: a lost customer, a fine, a re-do?

sources.name: Nielsen Norman Group — 10 usability heuristics
sources.why: The baseline vocabulary for reviewing any workspace screen.

sources.name: IBM Carbon Design System
sources.why: Enterprise patterns for data tables, forms, notifications and empty states, documented with usage guidance.

sources.name: GitHub Primer
sources.why: Patterns from a tool people work in all day: navigation, lists, empty states, saving.

sources.name: GOV.UK Design System — patterns
sources.why: Researched patterns for questions, errors and confirmation, tested with real users.
